title: 22. Interview: Distributed Systems Basics
summary: Interview Q&A for Distributed Systems Basics — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Distributed Systems Basics interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a distributed system and why is "only by passing messages" the crucial phrase?
**Answer:** A distributed system is a set of autonomous machines that cooperate to deliver a service whose correctness depends on coordination rather than shared memory. The word "only" matters because it rules out the convenient primitives a single-process program relies on: shared variables, mutexes, atomic test-and-set, and a single global clock. The moment processes communicate by sending bytes over a wire, three new failure modes appear: messages can be lost, messages can be delayed arbitrarily, and a peer that does not reply might be slow rather than dead. Every higher-level abstraction — leader election, distributed locks, replicated logs, consensus — exists to rebuild on top of this unreliable substrate the guarantees that a single process gets for free. Understanding this is what lets you reason about why a distributed lock is not the same as a `pthread_mutex`, why a distributed counter is not the same as `i++`, and why a "global timestamp" is a much harder problem than calling `time.time()`.
**Visual:**
```
shared memory:        message passing:
+--------+--------+   +------+   msg   +------+
| proc A | proc B |   |  A   | -------> |  B   |
+---+----+---+----+   +------+         +------+
    |  shared |
    +-- var --+
```

### Q2. State the eight fallacies of distributed computing and give one real outage each illustrates.
**Answer:** Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun listed: (1) the network is reliable — illustrated by the 2017 AWS S3 us-east-1 outage triggered by a typo that took an accounting subsystem offline; (2) latency is zero — every cross-region Cassandra query that exceeds a 100ms page-render budget; (3) bandwidth is infinite — the 2018 Cloudflare incident where a misconfigured parser saturated inter-DC links; (4) the network is secure — the 2016 Dyn DDoS that took down Twitter, Reddit and Netflix DNS; (5) topology doesn't change — Kubernetes pod churn breaking service-mesh sidecars; (6) there is one administrator — split-brain in multi-team etcd clusters where two operators resize concurrently; (7) transport cost is zero — egress charges that quietly dwarf compute bills; (8) the network is homogeneous — hybrid on-prem/cloud latency variance breaking Raft elections. The fallacies are not theoretical; they are a pre-mortem checklist every architect carries mentally.
**Visual:**
```
1 reliable    2 zero-latency   3 infinite-BW    4 secure
5 fixed-topo  6 one-admin      7 free-transport 8 homogeneous
   (assume none of the above -- price in every one)
```

### Q3. What is partial failure and why does it make distributed systems harder than concurrent single-machine programs?
**Answer:** Partial failure is the state where some components of a distributed system fail while others continue to operate. On a single machine a crash is binary — either the process is alive or it is dead, and the OS cleans up resources atomically. In a distributed system a node can be alive but unreachable, reachable but slow, slow but functional, or functional but lying (Byzantine). The other nodes cannot distinguish these states quickly because the only signal — lack of response — is identical across them. This forces every protocol to make a choice: wait forever for confirmation (liveness loss), proceed without confirmation (safety risk), or use timeouts and accept that they may declare a healthy node dead (false positives). Two-phase commit, Raft, Paxos and gossip protocols are all engineered around this ambiguity. The practical consequence is that distributed code has an entire dimension of error handling — network partitions, quorum loss, leader election — that local code does not, and this is why a "simple" distributed feature is often an order of magnitude more engineering work than its local equivalent.
**Visual:**
```
single machine:    ALIVE  |  DEAD           (binary, atomic)
distributed:       ALIVE | SLOW | CRASHED | PARTITIONED | BYZANTINE
                   (5 states, indistinguishable from outside)
```

### Q4. Explain CAP and PACELC in one breath and give a CP/EL and an AP/EL example.
**Answer:** CAP says that during a network Partition you must choose between Consistency (linearizability) and Availability; PACELC adds that *else* (when there is no partition) you still choose between Latency and Consistency. Google Spanner is CP/EL: it uses TrueTime and Paxos groups to remain linearizable even under partition, and pays a commit-wait latency cost normally. Amazon DynamoDB in its eventual-reads mode is AP/EL: it prefers availability during partitions and prefers low latency otherwise, returning stale-but-fast reads. MongoDB with writeConcern `majority` and readConcern `linearizable` sits closer to CP/EL, while Cassandra at `ONE`/`ONE` is firmly AP/EL. The theorem does not say one choice is better — it says the choice is unavoidable and that pretending to escape it (the secret fourth option) is the most common architect mistake. Pick the model that matches your business's tolerance for staleness versus the cost of refusing requests, and make the choice per subsystem, not per cluster.
**Visual:**
```
           partition?            yes                no
                |               CAP                 ELC
                |              /  \                /  \
                |             C    A              L    C
        Spanner ---------> CP / EL    (linearizable, TrueTime)
        DynamoDB --------> AP / EL    (eventual, low p99)
```

### Q5. Why can you not trust wall-clock time across nodes, and what do logical clocks buy you?
**Answer:** Wall clocks drift because quartz oscillators vary with temperature, NTP synchronization is bounded but not exact, and even GPS-locked clocks have residual uncertainty (Spanner's TrueTime bounds it to ~7ms but does not eliminate it). If two replicas both stamp a write with `time.time()` and their clocks disagree by 200ms, last-write-wins resolution will silently pick the wrong winner. Logical clocks solve the ordering problem without trusting wall time. Lamport clocks assign each event a counter `L = max(L_local, L_message) + 1`, giving a partial order that respects causality. Vector clocks extend this with a per-node counter, letting you detect concurrent writes explicitly and route them to application-level conflict resolution. The trade-off is that logical clocks tell you *happens-before* relationships but not *when* something happened in human time, so audit UIs and billing still need wall clocks. The right pattern is to keep both: a logical clock for ordering and conflict detection, plus a wall-clock timestamp for human display, never using the latter for correctness.
**Visual:**
```
wall clock:    A=10:00:00.001  B=10:00:00.200   (drift -> LWW wrong)
Lamport:       A=L3            B=L5              (causal, no drift)
vector:        A=[3,0,0]       B=[0,5,0]         (concurrent -> resolve)
```

### Q6. What is the difference between a crash-stop, crash-recovery and Byzantine failure model?
**Answer:** A crash-stop node either responds correctly or stops forever — once it fails it never recovers; this is the simplest model used in classic Paxos proofs. A crash-recovery node can fail and then come back, possibly with its disk intact (crash-recovery with stable storage) or wiped (crash-recovery without); Raft, etcd and ZooKeeper assume this model and use persistent logs to recover state. A Byzantine node can do anything — including lying, equivocating, or sending contradictory messages to different peers — which is the model assumed by Proof-of-Work blockchains, PBFT-based permissioned chains and aerospace flight-control networks. The cost scales dramatically: tolerating `f` crash failures needs `2f+1` nodes, while tolerating `f` Byzantine failures needs `3f+1`. For most enterprise infrastructure (Kafka, Redis Cluster, etcd) crash-recovery is the assumed model because the cost of Byzantine tolerance is rarely justified by the threat model, but financial systems and chains like Hyperledger Fabric do pay it.
**Visual:**
```
crash-stop:     alive -> dead              (2f+1 nodes for f faults)
crash-recovery: alive -> dead -> alive     (2f+1, persistent log)
byzantine:      alive -> arbitrary         (3f+1, signed messages)
```

### Q7. Why is idempotency such an important design principle in distributed systems?
**Answer:** Because the network may deliver a request once, never, or many times, and the only way to make "at-least-once" delivery safe is to make every operation idempotent so that retries have the same effect as a single execution. Payment systems attach a client-supplied idempotency key so a retried POST to `/charge` returns the original result instead of double-charging; Kafka producers use `ProducerId` plus a sequence number per partition to let brokers deduplicate retries; Kubernetes API server uses resource-version optimistic concurrency so a retried `update` either succeeds or returns `409 Conflict`, never silently overwrites. Without idempotency, every retry becomes a potential bug — a retry storm can multiply writes, send duplicate emails, or double-spend inventory. With idempotency, you can layer retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers freely because the worst case is wasted work, not corrupted state. This is why idempotency is the most leveraged ten lines of code you will ever add to a service.
**Visual:**
```
non-idempotent:   POST /charge  -> charge again -> $$$ lost
idempotent:       POST /charge  key=abc  -> same result on retry
dedupe layer:     id_table: {abc -> txn_001}  (PK constraint)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing Uber's trip-state service. During a network partition between the API gateway and the trip-state Cassandra cluster, do you choose CP or AP for (a) requesting a ride and (b) recording drop-off? Justify.
**Answer:** Requesting a ride should be AP: refusing a rider because a partition blocked a quorum write loses revenue and pushes riders to competitors; a brief window of slightly-stale supply visibility is acceptable, and the matching algorithm can re-evaluate within seconds. Recording drop-off should be CP-with-acknowledged-retry: dropping a drop-off event risks charging the wrong fare, losing driver payout, or double-charging a rider, so the system should hold the write locally (idempotently queued on the driver app), retry on reconnect, and only confirm completion after the durable store acknowledges a quorum write. Cassandra's tunable consistency supports both — `ONE` for the request path and `QUORUM` or `LOCAL_QUORUM` for the drop-off write, with a client-side idempotency key derived from trip_id + event_id. The pattern is the architect's bread and butter: pick a consistency level per operation, not per cluster, and make the cost of staleness explicit per use case.
**Visual:**
```
rider request ---> cassandra ONE        (AP, accept stale supply)
dropoff event ---> kafka + cassandra Q  (CP, idempotent retry)
                     ^                ^
                  revenue       billing integrity
```

### Q2. Netflix runs an active-active multi-region deployment of its playback service. A region pair loses connectivity for 90 seconds. Walk through what happens to playback resume positions.
**Answer:** Netflix stores playback resume positions in Cassandra with `LOCAL_QUORUM` writes and `LOCAL_ONE` reads, accepting that during a region partition the two regions diverge for that window. Each region keeps serving playback locally — no user is interrupted — and resume positions are written to the local Cassandra ring with a `last_modified` timestamp. When the partition heals, Cassandra's read-repair and hint handoff propagate the writes, and the more recent timestamp wins per row (last-write-wins). Because region-pair RTT is ~80ms and NTP drift is tightly controlled, LWW is safe for resume positions even though it would be unsafe for billing-grade data. The trade-off is that a user who pauses on their phone in region A and immediately opens a TV in region B might see a stale resume point for up to the convergence window — an acceptable UX cost compared to the alternative of refusing writes and breaking playback. The key design choice was classifying resume-position data as eventually-consistent from day one.
**Visual:**
```
region A: pause at 12:30  (LWW ts=1001)
region B: partition  90s
   ...both serve playback, both write locally...
heal: read-repair + hint handoff
winner: ts=1001  (region A)  -> converges across both rings
```

### Q3. You inherit a Kafka cluster where producers set `acks=0` to hit 1M msgs/sec. The on-call team reports intermittent data loss when brokers restart. Diagnose and prescribe a fix.
**Answer:** `acks=0` means the producer considers a send successful the moment it leaves the socket — there is no broker acknowledgement, no retry on leader change, and no durability guarantee if the leader crashes before flushing to disk. When a broker restarts, in-flight messages buffered in its OS page cache or in the leader's log-not-yet-flushed are lost. The fix is to switch to `acks=all` (broker-level `min.insync.replicas=2`), which means the leader waits for all in-sync replicas to acknowledge before responding to the producer; combined with `retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5`, `enable.idempotence=true`, and a producer `delivery.timeout.ms` budget, this gives exactly-once semantics within a partition at the cost of higher p99 latency. For the use case where 1M msgs/sec is non-negotiable, partition more aggressively, add brokers, and tune `linger.ms` and `batch.size` to amortize the ack cost — but never trade correctness for throughput by dropping acks entirely. The original choice was almost certainly a load-test artifact shipped to production.
**Visual:**
```
acks=0:  producer -> broker   (fire and forget, LOSSY)
acks=1:  producer -> leader    ack    (loses on leader crash)
acks=all: producer -> leader+ISR ack  (durable, slower)
```

### Q4. A Kubernetes cluster's kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager both think they are the leader. Pods are being scheduled twice. What distributed-systems primitive has failed and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** This is split-brain in the leader-election layer. Kubernetes components use a lease object in etcd with `leader-election-renew-deadline` and `leader-election-lease-duration` to elect a single active instance; if the apiserver is unreachable from one candidate (partition) but reachable from the other, both may briefly believe they hold the lease, and both will issue scheduling decisions. The root cause is almost always either a clock skew between the candidates and etcd, an apiserver overload that makes the lease-renew heartbeat miss its deadline, or an etcd quorum loss in the underlying Raft cluster. The immediate fix is to identify and fence one of the contenders — usually by stopping the duplicate process — and let the lease expire. The structural fix is to ensure etcd has an odd number of members and a healthy quorum, that NTP is locked on all control-plane nodes, that lease durations exceed the worst-case apiserver RTT, and that the scheduler uses optimistic concurrency (`resourceVersion`) so a duplicate scheduling attempt produces a `409 Conflict` instead of a double-bind. Leader election is not a substitute for idempotent writes.
**Visual:**
```
etcd quorum ok:        scheduler-1 LEADER, scheduler-2 STANDBY
etcd partition:        scheduler-1 thinks LEADER, scheduler-2 thinks LEADER
                       -> double-bind pod X to node A AND node B
fix: resourceVersion 409 on second bind; fence stale contender
```

### Q5. Instagram migrated from a sharded PostgreSQL primary to a Cassandra ring for Direct Messaging inbox metadata. What distributed-systems properties of Cassandra made this the right call, and what did they give up?
**Answer:** Cassandra offers multi-datacenter replication with tunable consistency per query, no single point of failure (every node is peers), linear horizontal scalability via consistent hashing, and writes that are always fast (append to commit log + memtable). For a high-write, eventually-consistent inbox workload where 100ms of staleness is invisible to the user, these properties let Instagram absorb traffic spikes without reshuffling shards or worrying about a single primary failing over. They gave up strong consistency: a user could see a message in one device and not another for a brief convergence window, and conflict resolution relies on timestamps so clock skew must be tightly controlled. They also gave up SQL joins — inbox queries had to be modeled as wide rows keyed by `(user_id, message_id)` rather than normalized tables. The lesson is that the migration worked because the workload's tolerance for eventual consistency was high, and the data model was redesigned for the new system rather than ported.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL sharded:      strong, joins, manual reshard, SPOF per shard
Cassandra ring:          eventual, denormalized, auto-rebalance, no SPOF
                         (gained: scale, HA, multi-DC; lost: SQL, linearizability)
```

### Q6. WhatsApp handles 100B+ messages a day with an Erlang cluster of thousands of nodes. A node hosting a popular group chat crashes mid-broadcast. How do you ensure no messages are lost or duplicated?
**Answer:** Erlang's per-process model maps naturally to per-chat actors: each group chat lives on one node as a process holding the member list and a monotonic sequence number per recipient. When a client sends a message it includes the last sequence number it saw; the server rejects gaps and forces the client to backfill. On send, the chat process writes the message to a durable queue (Erlang's `mnesia` or a backing store) before acknowledging the sender, so a crash after ack is safe. When the chat process crashes, Erlang's supervisor restarts it on another node, recovers state from the durable queue, and resumes broadcasting to any recipient whose acknowledgement is still outstanding. Clients retry with the same client-supplied message id, and the server deduplicates against the queue so retries produce one delivery. The combination — at-least-once network delivery, idempotent server-side dedupe, durable per-entity queues, and supervised restart — gives the user exactly-once semantics without paying the latency of distributed transactions.
**Visual:**
```
client send msg(id=42) -> chat_process
chat_process:  enqueue(42) -> broadcast(recipients) -> ack(client)
crash before ack: client retries id=42
new chat_process: enqueue(42) -> duplicate detected -> skip broadcast -> ack
```

### Q7. YouTube transcodes uploaded videos across thousands of workers using a work-queue. A worker crashes after transcoding a 4K chunk but before marking the task done. Design the recovery without re-transcoding the world.
**Answer:** Treat transcoding as idempotent with content-addressed outputs. Each task is keyed by `(video_id, chunk_hash, rendition_profile)` and writes its output to GCS under a deterministic path derived from that key. A worker, on startup or task lease, checks whether the output object already exists and its size matches the expected; if so, it just marks the task done without re-transcoding. The task queue uses lease-with-heartbeat: a worker takes a task, gets a 10-minute lease, and renews every 2 minutes; if it crashes, the lease expires and another worker picks up the task, finds the existing output, and short-circuits. For chunks that were only partially written, GCS multipart uploads abort on lease expiry and the partial upload is garbage collected, so the next attempt starts clean. The pattern is universal in distributed batch systems — MapReduce, Spark, Airflow — and the core insight is that idempotency plus content-addressed storage turns a crash-recovery problem into a check-and-skip problem.
**Visual:**
```
task: (video=V, chunk=H, profile=p144)
worker-1: lease 10min -> transcode -> write gs://out/V/H/p144 (in progress)
          crash before commit  -> lease expires
worker-2: lease 10min -> HEAD gs://out/V/H/p144
          exists + size ok?  -> mark task done, skip work
          partial?           -> abort multipart, re-transcode
```
